w: Buried by the same 79 AD eruption that took Pompeii, Herculaneum got the stranger fate: a pyroclastic flow carbonized wood instead of burying it in ash, so roofs and doors survived intact. Treasure hunters tunnelled in from 1709; real digging began in 1738, and most of the wealthy seaside town stays buried still.
s: The town Vesuvius carbonized instead of merely burying
_facts: Ancient Roman town in modern Ercolano, Campania, buried by pyroclastic flow in the 79 AD Vesuvius eruption
Volcanic material carbonized wood (roofs, beds, doors) and preserved organics unlike ash-buried Pompeii
Rediscovered by chance in 1709 during well drilling; treasure seekers tunnelled and took artifacts before regular excavation began in 1738
Was a wealthy seaside retreat for the Roman elite, population ~5,000; only a fraction is excavated, with focus now on preservation

w: Charles of Bourbon built this seaside palace minutes from Herculaneum's ruins, then made it home to the Accademia Ercolanese in 1758 - the first museum built to house finds dug from the buried city next door. Royal apartments, a Chinese Room and frescoed antechambers survive, alongside its old botanical garden.
s: A palace built to house what Herculaneum gave up
_facts: Former royal palace in Portici, southeast of Naples, Campania, a few hundred metres from the Herculaneum ruins
Now a museum complex: royal apartments, Herculanense Museum, frescoed antechambers, Chinese Room, historical library, and the Orto Botanico di Portici
Seat of the Accademia Ercolanese, established 1758 by Charles VII of Naples, originally holding finds from Herculaneum, Pompeii and Stabiae excavations
Once part of a larger royal estate that included an English garden, a zoo and formal parterres

w: Founded in 1841 by Ferdinand II on the volcano's own slopes, the Osservatorio Vesuviano is the oldest volcanology institute on Earth - built to watch the mountain that had buried two Roman cities. Its Naples operations sit inside Italy's geophysics institute, still watching Vesuvius, the Phlegraean Fields and Ischia.
_facts: Surveillance centre for Vesuvius, the Phlegraean Fields and Ischia in Campania, Italy
Founded 1841 on the slopes of Mount Vesuvius by Ferdinand II of Bourbon, King of the Two Sicilies
The oldest volcanology institute in the world
Current operative centre based in Naples, hosting a section of the National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology
